html:
The map's label for the peoples of the Pampas, the flat grasslands of what is now central Argentina and Uruguay, shown from 1500 BCE to 1815.

Before the Spanish came they were hunter-gatherers. They hunted guanaco, rhea and deer with bows and with bolas, stones tied to cords and thrown to tangle an animal's legs. Groups included the Querandí near the Río de la Plata, the Charrúa in Uruguay, and to the south the Puelche and Tehuelche.

In 1536 the Spaniard Pedro de Mendoza founded the first Buenos Aires. The Querandí resisted, food ran out, and the settlement was abandoned in 1541. It was founded again in 1580.

The Spanish brought horses and cattle that ran wild and multiplied on the grass, part of the Columbian Exchange. By the 1600s the Pampas peoples had become mounted hunters and raiders. They drove cattle across the Andes to sell in Chile, and from the 1700s the Mapuche spread their language, trade and chiefdoms east across the plains. The colony traded with them and built frontier forts, and the grasslands bred the mules sent to Peru.

For most of the period on the map these peoples stayed independent of Spanish America. Argentina conquered them only in the Conquest of the Desert of 1878 to 1885.
sum: The map's label for the peoples of the Pampas, the flat grasslands of what is now central Argentina and Uruguay, shown from 1500 BCE to 1815.
